newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Aid bodies brief U.N. council on Africa crisis.
newsitem.headline: Aid bodies brief U.N. council on Africa crisis.

text.p: Representatives of three humanitarian organisations urged the Security Council on Wednesday to give priority to the crisis in the Great Lakes region of Central Africa and enable aid groups to gain access to refugees.

"We discussed at some length our concerns over the last three years that, whereas there had been considerable humanitarian activity, there had not always been political activity to match that, " David Bryer, the director of OXFAM, said.
"And we felt sometimes we were a fig leaf while the member states of the U.N. were not playing their full part on the political side," he added.

Bryer was speaking to reporters after representatives of his organisation, CARE and Medecins sans Frontieres (Doctors without Borders) held a briefing for members of the Security Council and other U.N. bodies.

Noting there had been well over a million deaths in the region as a result of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda and bloodshed in Burundi and Zaire, he said the situation was "five times worse than in Yugoslavia" and required a response commensurate with what the world body did there.
"It needed to be at the top of the international agenda," he added.

Pierre Salignon, a field coordinator for Medecins sans Frontieres, said more than 120,000 refugees in Tingi Tingi camp in East Zaire faced a major lack of food and the front-line between the Zaire army and rebels was coming increasingly close.
Calling for protection for the most vulnerable among the refugees, he suggested the possibility of moving them to a safer place.

Bryer said that without guaranteed security zones, it was not feasible to carry out humanitarian operations, especially in Burundi but increasingly in Rwanda and in certain parts of Zaire's Kivu province.
Marc Lindenberg, senior vice-president of CARE, said humanitarian action was not a substitute for political and economic solutions.

He said Security Council members were strongly urged to provide full backing and resources for Mohammed Sahnoun, the Algerian diplomat recently appointed jointly by the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity as trouble-shooter for the Great Lakes region.
